title: Who Shares What From Whom: An Ego-Network Conjoint of Misinformation Sharing
summary: This study asks how the type of information, and who shares it, shape willingness to share a post and judgments of its plausibility. We ran a conjoint experiment with 12,000 profiles from US Latino (Hispanic) adults in a YouGov sample, surveyed in English or Spanish. Only the headline type was randomized; the sharer's tie strength, origin, ideology, trust, knowledge and belief in disputed claims are measured attributes of the respondent's real contacts. Compared with true or neutral headlines, misinformation was chosen 18.2 points less often (95% CI [−20.4, −16.0]) and fact-checks 13.3 points less often (95% CI [−15.6, −11.1]). A2. Sharing without believing: among profiles chosen to share, the probability that the respondent judged the other post more plausible, by information type, net of source attributes, media trust and age. — Misinformation

A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. — Congruent

A3. Co-ideological messenger: sharing when the respondent and the sharer lean the same way (both liberal or both conservative) against opposite leans; pairs involving a moderate form a third group. Cell differences, no controls. — Neutral (a moderate)

A4. Ego-network composition: the respondent's six named contacts as a measured network. Among misinformation profiles, sharing on the network's mean perceived belief in disputed claims, net of network ideological spread, mean trust, age and ideology. Each misinformation profile is weighted by 1 / the respondent's number of them, which reproduces the respondent-level regression of the misinformation-sharing rate.

extensions.label: Design advance
extensions.why: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.
extensions.title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
extensions.hypothesis: Source trust and tie strength raise sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, especially for the false headline.
extensions.primary_outcome: Sharing intent (1-7) minus perceived accuracy (1-7, standardized), and each rating separately.

extensions.label: Generalizability
extensions.why: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.
extensions.title: Replication across populations and languages
extensions.hypothesis: The misinformation sharing penalty is negative in all groups, and it is smaller among Spanish-language Latino respondents than among English-language Latino respondents. High sharer trust is associated with more sharing in all groups.
extensions.primary_outcome: Chosen to share (1 if the headline was chosen in 'Which post would you be more likely to share?')

extensions.label: Theoretical debate
extensions.why: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.
extensions.title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
extensions.hypothesis: If sharing follows belief, the source effect on sharing equals its effect on accuracy. If identity drives sharing, the co-ideological source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy, especially for false headlines and among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims.
extensions.primary_outcome: Difference between sharing intent and accuracy rating (both standardized), by source condition, headline veracity and belief tertile.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running. The headline result is solid: misinformation is shared and believed about 18 points less, and the study's main gap is causal inference about sources, since every sharer attribute was measured rather than assigned. Run Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures first. It randomizes trust and tie, which carried the only notable sharer signals (+5.7 and +3.0 points), and it separates sharing from belief, which the forced-choice outcomes here conflate. The belief-versus-identity design comes second and the cross-population replication third.
debates: Is sharing misinformation driven by belief?
